title: If I perish (Esther 4:16, 7)
hook: Esther says "if I perish, I perish", and names the enemy at her banquet

segments.voice: Yesterday, Mordecai asked Esther who knows whether she came to the palace for such a time as this. Your line was for such a time as this. Did you do your one thing? Today, Esther answers, and the week ends. Day eight hundred sixty-eight.

Esther's reply is short, and it's an order. Go, gather all the Jews in Shushan, and fast for me. Don't eat or drink for three days, night or day. My maids and I will fast too. Then I'll go in to the king, which is not according to the law. And she ends with a line that sounds almost like a shrug: "and if I perish, I perish." Something has flipped. Back in chapter two, Mordecai gave the orders and Esther kept quiet. Now the text says Mordecai went his way and "did according to all that Esther had commanded him."
screen: `FAST FOR ME, THREE DAYS.` → `NOT ACCORDING TO THE LAW.` → `NOW MORDECAI TAKES ORDERS.`

segments.voice: If I perish, I perish. It isn't despair. It's a person counting the cost before she moves, and then moving. Esther doesn't pretend the danger is small. She names it, prepares, and goes. On the third day she puts on her royal clothes and stands in the inner court. The king sees her, and holds out the golden scepter. She lives. He offers her anything, up to half the kingdom. And here's the surprise: she doesn't blurt out her request. She invites the king and Haman to a banquet. At the banquet, she invites them to another one. Some readers call it stalling. Others call it strategy: she's choosing the room, the hour, and the moment the king is ready to listen. At the second banquet, chapter seven, she finally speaks, and she ties her own life to her people's: "let my life be given me at my petition, and my people at my request." The secret she kept since chapter two, who her people are, is out loud now. "For we are sold, I and my people, to be destroyed, to be slain, and to perish." Perish again, the same word she risked for herself. The king asks who would dare. And she names him to his face: "The adversary and enemy is this wicked Haman." Before the chapter ends, Haman is hanged on the gallows he had built for Mordecai. The story still has chapters to run, but the turn happens here, at a dinner table, when one person says the name.
screen: `COUNT THE COST, THEN MOVE.` · then, large: `IF I PERISH, I PERISH.` · `TWO BANQUETS BEFORE SHE SPEAKS.` · `I AND MY PEOPLE.` · then: `THIS WICKED HAMAN.`

segments.voice: Before the bell, a look back at this week. Mercies new every morning. Renew our days. Vashti's no. The secret Esther kept. A man who wouldn't bow. Mordecai's question. And today's answer. Now the practice: speak up for someone. Bring to mind one person who isn't in the room when things about them get decided. A coworker, a neighbor, a child, someone easy to forget. What would you say for them, if you were asked? Find the sentence. Make it plain and kind and true. Esther took three days to get ready; you have the length of the bell. If you pray, you can hold that person before God in words from your tradition. The bell holds the time.
If I perish. Esther's words before she goes in to the king uncalled: counting the cost, and going anyway. Today's word.
Your line: if I perish, I perish. Today, say the sentence you found, to someone who can do something with it. Day eight hundred sixty-eight.

howItsDone: The day before Purim is kept by tradition as the Fast of Esther, Ta'anit Esther, which recalls the fast she asked of the Jews of Shushan before she went in to the king.

what it means: Esther counts the cost, prepares with three days of fasting, and goes in uncalled anyway.
what a scholar hears: perish comes back in chapter seven, when she says her people are sold to perish. she risks for herself what her people face.
